leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial (via Rose Street)
name: Rose Street (West End)
address: Rose Street at South Charlotte Street, Edinburgh
description: This thousand-metre run of pubs, bars and restaurants, and you're standing at the start of what Victorian Edinburgh called faintly disreputable after dark - the street its own pub crawl nicknamed the 'Amber Mile'. Laid out by James Craig in 1767 as a modest service lane behind George Street's grand townhouses, it's this trade character, not the architecture, that made Rose Street famous. The crawl traditionally starts right here on your left at Scott's, 202 Rose Street - dating to 1790, named for a formidable 19th-century landlady, 'Ma Scott', still advertised on the pub's own sign today.

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial (via Rose Street)
name: Charlotte Chapel / Rose Theatre
description: This plain, dignified stone hall, and you'd never guess it once held a Baptist congregation of 1,000 - or that it's now a four-stage theatre. Built in 1912 to a design by J A Arnott and J Inch Morrison, this was Charlotte Chapel, founded in January 1808 by evangelist Christopher Anderson, who began preaching in the Pleasance before outgrowing that hall and relocating here. Its restrained exterior gives little away about the busy life that has filled it for over two centuries.

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial (via Rose Street)
name: Beachcomber by George Mackay Brown
description: The arched windows of this former telephone exchange reward a slow read as you pass - seven laser-cut steel panels, each illustrating one verse of Orcadian poet George Mackay Brown's 1971 poem 'Beachcomber'. Artist Astrid Jaekel designed the piece first as intricate hand-cut paper before Pentland Precision Engineering translated it into weatherproof steel, commissioned around 2012-13 by Essential Edinburgh as a nod to the 'Rose Street Poets' who once drank in its pubs.

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial (via Rose Street)
name: Rose Street's Last Original Block
description: This long run of matching three-storey-and-attic buildings, and you're looking at the only stretch of Rose Street where the original terraced rhythm survives unbroken end to end. Put up around 1790 as plain coursed-rubble tenements with shops let in at street level, Historic Environment Scotland lists numbers 172 to 202 together as a single Category B entry - 'a significant surviving part of the original fabric' of the New Town.

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial (via Rose Street)
name: Rose Street's First Pedestrianised Stretch
address: Rose Street at Castle Street, Edinburgh
description: The paving beneath your feet on this block, and you're standing on a small piece of Edinburgh planning history - in 1973 it became the first street in the city closed to traffic and paved for pedestrians only, years ahead of Rose Street's other blocks or even Princes Street. In the 1980s, artist Maggy Howarth set eight large circular pebble mosaics into the surface at its side-street junctions, each a different rose design worked entirely from small stones, sturdy enough to carry delivery vans.

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial (via Rose Street)
name: McVitie's Original Shop
description: This unremarkable shopfront marks where one of Britain's best-known biscuit makers began. In 1830, Robert McVitie ran a modest provision shop from here, baking and selling bread and confectionery to Rose Street's working trade decades before the family name became a household word - one workshop among many that gave the street its tradesman's character in the shadow of George Street's banks.

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial (via Rose Street)
name: The Kenilworth
description: Behind this unassuming Rose Street frontage are blue-and-white Minton tiles running floor-to-ceiling under brown-and-white banding, beneath a patterned red-and-cream plasterwork ceiling. The building dates to around 1780, but the ornate interior you're standing in is the work of architect Thomas Purves Marwick, fitted out in 1899 and trading as the Kenilworth by 1904, named for Sir Walter Scott's 1821 novel. It's Category A listed - Rose Street's highest heritage grade.

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial
name: Alexander Graham Bell Birthplace
description: A green door with a small carved plaque beside it marks the flat where Alexander Graham Bell was born on 3 March 1847. His father, Alexander Melville Bell, was a renowned elocutionist who ran a school from here training teachers of the deaf using his own 'Visible Speech' system - work the young Bell grew up around, and would later echo in Boston. Both his mother and, eventually, his wife were deaf, a thread that ran through his life long before the invention that made him famous.

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial
name: St John's Episcopal Church
address: St John's Church, Princes Street, Edinburgh EH2 4BJ
description: Inside, the plaster fan-vaulted ceiling, modelled on the Henry VII Chapel at Westminster Abbey - the single most striking feature of this Gothic Revival church marking the western gateway into Princes Street Gardens. Architect William Burn was only 25 when he designed it; building began in 1816 and it was dedicated as St John's Chapel on Maundy Thursday 1818. An Act of Parliament passed the same year banned any further building on the north side of Princes Street, specifically to protect views of the Castle.

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial
name: St Cuthbert's Parish Church
description: This churchyard, tucked just below St John's, sits on ground worshipped continuously for longer than almost anywhere else in Edinburgh. Tradition holds that St Cuthbert founded a church here around AD 670, and the site is first documented in a charter of about 1127. The current building, opened in 1894 to a design by Hippolyte Blanc, is only the latest in a long line on this spot - when the previous Georgian church of 1775 was demolished, evidence of six earlier buildings beneath it was reportedly found.

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial
name: Ross Fountain
address: West Princes Street Gardens, Edinburgh EH1 2EU
description: Nude and semi-nude figures rise in three tiers above you - an unlikely sight beneath Edinburgh Castle's ramparts. Cast in ornate French Second Empire style at the Durenne foundry in France and shown at the 1862 International Exhibition in London, Edinburgh gunmaker Daniel Ross bought it for £2,000 and gave it to the city. Shipped north to Leith in 122 separate pieces, it was bolted back together and installed here in 1872.

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial
name: Norwegian Memorial Stone
address: West Princes Street Gardens (terrace path near Castle Street), Edinburgh EH2 3AA
description: A weathered grey boulder of Norwegian gneiss sits beside the path, propped on three smaller stones of the same rock, a single inscription carved into it. It was presented to Edinburgh on 18 September 1978 by veterans of the Norwegian Brigade, the exiled force raised and trained in Scotland during the Second World War after Norway fell to German occupation in 1940. General Sir Roland Gibbs accepted it on behalf of the British Army, asking the Lord Provost to take the stone into the city's care.

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial
name: Scottish American War Memorial
address: West Princes Street Gardens (near Castle Street), Edinburgh EH2 3AP
description: A bronze kilted infantryman kneels before you, gazing toward Castle Rock, backed by a frieze of soldiers marching off behind a piper. Titled 'The Call 1914', it was sculpted by Robert Tait McKenzie, a Scottish-Canadian based at the University of Pennsylvania, and took him around four years to complete; the figures were cast at the Roman Bronze Works in Brooklyn before shipping to Scotland. It was unveiled on 7 September 1927 by the American Ambassador, Alanson B. Houghton.

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial
name: Wojtek the Soldier Bear Memorial
address: West Princes Street Gardens, Edinburgh (near Castle Street terrace path)
description: A bronze soldier walks beside a bear at one-and-a-quarter life size, one hand resting on its back - this is Wojtek - a Syrian brown bear cub bought from a boy in Iran in 1942 by Polish soldiers on their way to war. He grew up inside the 22nd Artillery Supply Company, drinking beer, wrestling the men and eating cigarettes. Unveiled on 7 November 2015, the memorial is the work of Scottish sculptor Alan Beattie Herriot, cast at Powderhall Bronze here in Edinburgh, with a bronze relief panel behind tracing his wartime journey.

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial (via Rose Street)
name: The Johnnie Walker Experience
description: This eight-storey building on the corner of Princes Street and Frederick Street is one of Scotland's most ambitious pieces of whisky tourism - an immersive experience built inside a completely remodelled former department store, opened to the public on 6 September 2021. Diageo, the drinks giant behind Johnnie Walker, poured £185 million into the project, the single largest investment ever made in Scotch whisky tourism, transforming the old Binns store into tasting rooms, interactive galleries and a rooftop bar looking straight across the city to Edinburgh Castle.

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial (via Rose Street)
name: Social Bite
description: This modest café is where the whole Social Bite movement began. In 2012, Josh Littlejohn and Alice Thompson opened it as a coffee shop that gave its profits to good causes - a straightforward idea that turned into something much bigger. Not long after opening, a young man named Peter, who had been selling The Big Issue outside, came in and asked for a job; hiring him convinced the founders to build supported employment for people with experience of homelessness into the heart of the business.

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial (via Rose Street)
name: Statue of the Royal Regiment of Scotland
address: West Princes Street Gardens, between the amphitheatre and Ross Fountain, Edinburgh
description: A reclining bronze lion sits in front of you, inspired directly by the Royal Regiment of Scotland's own cap badge, unveiled by King Charles III on 1 July 2026 - sited deliberately here between the amphitheatre and Ross Fountain, with the Regiment's headquarters at Edinburgh Castle as its backdrop. Sculptor Kenny Hunter cast the lion in six separate sections, each representing one of the six historic Scottish infantry regiments that amalgamated in 2006 to form the modern Royal Regiment of Scotland.

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial (via Rose Street)
name: Police Box Cafe
description: This pastel pink-and-green kiosk is one of Edinburgh's old police boxes - miniature one-person police stations that once stood on street corners across the city, now doing a brisk trade in coffee instead of crime-fighting. City architect Ebenezer MacRae designed the model from 1933, giving each box a pediment, pilasters and cast-iron panelling deliberately styled to blend into the New Town's neo-classical streetscape rather than stand out as municipal furniture.

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial (via Rose Street)
name: The Caledonian Hotel
description: Red sandstone rises above Princes Street here, quarried at Locharbriggs and Corncockle in Dumfriesshire and brought in on the Caledonian Railway Company's own trains. Built between 1899 and 1903 as the grand terminus hotel for Princes Street Station, arriving passengers could once step straight from the platforms through three archways into the hotel itself. Long known simply as 'The Caley', it outlived the station by decades: passenger trains stopped running in September 1965, but the hotel above kept operating.

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial (via Rose Street)
name: Dean Ramsay Memorial
address: St John's Episcopal Church, Princes Street, Edinburgh EH1 2EP
description: This soaring Celtic cross, over 8 metres of Shap granite on three broad steps, stands in the graveyard of St John's Episcopal Church. It commemorates Edward Bannerman Ramsay, the church's minister for over 40 years and Dean of Edinburgh from 1841 until his death in 1872. Designed by architect Robert Rowand Anderson and erected in 1879, the cross carries bronze relief panels cast by F. A. Skidmore of Coventry, depicting scenes from Christ's Passion alongside six acts of charity - fitting for a man remembered as much for his philanthropy as his ministry.

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial (via Rose Street)
name: Mather's Bar
description: This single-room corner bar has an interior that's changed remarkably little in well over a century - high ceilings with ornate plasterwork, a large stained-glass window, floor-to-ceiling tiling in the porch, and an original bar counter and half-height panelling. Wine merchant Hugh Mather took over the ground floor of this 1900 building in 1902 and established the licensed premises the following year, giving the pub its name, still running in gold lettering across the frontage: 'Wines. H.P. Mather. Spirits.'

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial (via Rose Street)
name: Statue of Sir James Young Simpson
description: This seated bronze figure in academic robes, book resting on one knee, erected by public subscription in 1877 and designed by sculptor William Brodie. It commemorates Sir James Young Simpson, professor of midwifery at Edinburgh University, who in November 1847 became the first doctor to demonstrate chloroform's use as an anaesthetic - testing it first on himself and two colleagues at his own dinner table before adopting it in his obstetric practice. The discovery transformed surgery and childbirth almost overnight.

leg: Bute House -> Wojtek Memorial (via Rose Street)
name: Princes Street
description: Here's the oddity: Edinburgh's most famous street has buildings running down only one side of it. James Craig's 1767 plan left the north side of Princes Street open on purpose, so residents - and later, everyone - would keep an unbroken view south across the valley to the Old Town and the Castle on its crag. That valley used to be underwater, the old Nor Loch, drained as the New Town went up, and its bed became Princes Street Gardens - still open ground today for exactly the reason Craig intended.
